arguments.content: EMERGENCY MOTION FOR TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER AND ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE WHY A PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION SHOULD NOT ISSUE. Plaintiff Meridian Technologies Inc. respectfully requests that this Court enter a TRO pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. This conduct threatens irreparable harm to Plaintiff’s ability to prosecute its claims for breach of contract and misappropriation of trade secrets under New York law and the Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1836. Plaintiff requests expedited hearing and service.

arguments.court: US District Court, Eastern District of Texas
arguments.content:
MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT

I. INTRODUCTION
This action arises from a commercial dispute over a software licensing agreement between Meridian Technologies Inc. and Apex Global Solutions LLC. Plaintiff seeks $4.2 million in damages for alleged breach of contract. For the reasons set forth below, Defendant is entitled to summary judgment under Fed. R. Civ. P. 56 because there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and Defendant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

II. LEGAL STANDARD
Under Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986), the moving party need not negate the opponent’s claim but must demonstrate the absence of a genuine issue of material fact. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986), requires that the evidence be viewed in the light most favorable to the non-moving party. However, where the record taken as a whole could not lead a rational trier of fact to find for the non-moving party, summary judgment is appropriate.

III. ANALYSIS
A. Enforceability of Licensing Agreement
The software license at issue is governed by UCC Article 2 as adopted under federal diversity jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1332). The agreement contains valid offer, acceptance, and consideration. Plaintiff accepted the terms electronically, satisfying formation requirements.

B. Limitation of Liability Clause
Section 8.3 of the agreement caps liability at 12 months of fees paid and excludes consequential damages. This limitation is enforceable under Delaware law (governing law per Section 14.1) and bars Plaintiff’s claim for lost profits, which constitute consequential damages.

C. Indemnification and Non-Compete Provisions
While Plaintiff asserts breach of indemnification obligations (Section 8.1), the clause is mutual under redlined terms negotiated in good faith. Moreover, Plaintiff has not demonstrated any third-party claims triggering indemnity. The non-compete (Section 12.1) is narrowly tailored to protect legitimate business interests and does not preclude Plaintiff from operating in unrelated markets.

D. No Genuine Dispute of Material Fact
Discovery has closed (see docket entry DL-001). No evidence has been produced showing Defendant failed to perform under the agreement or that damages exceed the contractual cap. Plaintiff’s claims are speculative and fail to meet the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

IV. CONCLUSION
Defendant respectfully requests that this Court grant summary judgment in its favor and dismiss all claims with prejudice.

Respectfully submitted,
Harrison Blackwell PC
Counsel for Defendant
